idea_angle: A one-sitting New Year money reset in seven steps: snapshot, last year's real spending, a three-line budget, one savings rate, a debt order, sinking funds, and a quarterly check-in.

script.title: The 2027 money reset: a complete plan in one sitting
script.hook: 7 steps, about an hour, and your whole 2027 money plan is done before January really starts.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Seven steps, about an hour, and your whole money plan for 2027 is done. Not a resolution you'll forget by February, a system that runs on its own. We'll take a snapshot of where you are, look at what last year actually cost, build a three-line budget, pick one savings rate, put your debts in order, set up sinking funds for the costs you already know are coming, and book four check-ins. Grab your banking app, your card statements and something to write on.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes at a kitchen table with a laptop, a notebook and a mug, January calendar on the wall. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 1: snapshot
segments.narration: Step one: a snapshot. Write down every account balance: checking, savings, retirement, investments. Then every debt: cards, student loans, car loan. Subtract what you owe from what you own. That's your net worth today. If it's negative, that's normal in your twenties, especially with student loans. This number isn't a grade. It's the starting line, so next January you can see how far you moved.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a balance scale with small jars on one side and papers on the other. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2: last year
segments.narration: Step two: what did last year actually cost? Don't guess. Open your bank and card apps and look at the last three months. Add up four things: fixed bills, food including eating out, transportation, and everything else. Multiply by four for a rough year. Most people find one category that's far bigger than they thought. Circle it. That's where this year's plan has the most room.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a bar chart with four bars, one much taller and circled. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3: three lines
segments.narration: Step three: the budget, in three lines. Line one, bills: every fixed cost, on autopay. Line two, savings: one automatic transfer the day after payday. Line three, everything else: what's left, divided by the weeks in the month. That weekly number is the only thing you track. Example: thirty-two hundred take-home, eighteen-fifty bills, one-sixty savings, leaves about two hundred seventy-five a week. If that weekly number looks impossible, the fix is in line one, not in willpower.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a short note with three lines and a small weekly calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 4: savings rate
segments.narration: Step four: pick one savings rate for the year. That's savings divided by take-home. Five to ten percent is a strong start. Set the transfer now, and put a reminder on July first to raise it by one or two points. If your employer offers a 401(k) match, make sure you're contributing enough to get all of it. That's separate from your cash savings, and it's the closest thing to free money most people get.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a dial set to a modest mark with two coins dropping into a jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 5: debt order
segments.narration: Step five: put your debts in order. List each one with its balance, interest rate and minimum. Every minimum goes on autopay today. Then pick a method. Avalanche: extra money goes to the highest rate first, which saves the most interest. Snowball: smallest balance first, which gives quicker wins. Both work if you stick with them. Write down a debt-free date with a payoff calculator. A date makes it real.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a short ranked list with arrows and a small calendar flag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 6: sinking funds
segments.narration: Step six: sinking funds. These are the costs that feel like surprises but aren't: car registration, insurance renewals, gifts, travel, a wedding you're invited to. List the ones you know are coming this year with the month and amount. Divide each by the months until it's due. A six-hundred-dollar trip in June, starting in January, is a hundred a month. Start with the two that hurt most last year. You don't need all of them on day one.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a row of small labeled jars filling at different speeds. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 7: check-ins
segments.narration: Step seven: book four check-ins. End of March, June, September and December. Twenty minutes each. Update your net worth, check your savings rate, adjust the weekly number, and look at your debt-free date. That's it. Most plans fail not because they're wrong but because nobody looks at them again. Four calendar events fix that.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar with four circled dates. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: When it breaks
segments.narration: And when it breaks, because some week it will, don't wait for next month. Start from today's balance, reset the weekly number, and keep going. A budget that breaks and restarts is still working. The people who succeed with money aren't the ones who never slip. They're the ones who restart quickly.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes stepping back onto a path after a small stumble. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. One: snapshot your net worth. Two: find what last year really cost. Three: build a three-line budget. Four: pick one savings rate and get the full match. Five: autopay every minimum and pick avalanche or snowball. Six: sinking funds for known costs. Seven: book four check-ins. Do it once, this week, and 2027 mostly runs itself.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes checking the last box on a list with confetti. No text, no logos, no real people.

script.title: Rate My Budget: 3 budgets, fully broken down
script.hook: 3 budgets, 3 very different problems, and the same 5-question scorecard. Let's rate them.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Three budgets, three very different problems, and one scorecard. This is a long-form Rate My Budget. All three are fictional examples, built to show common patterns, not real people. We'll score each one out of ten using five questions, two points each: savings rate, housing share, high-rate debt, irregular costs, and automation. Then we'll fix them, with the math. Score your own budget as we go.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes with a clipboard in front of three small houses of different sizes. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The scorecard
segments.narration: Quick rules. Savings rate: two points at ten percent of take-home or more, one point above zero. Housing: two points if rent is up to about forty percent of take-home, one point up to fifty. High-rate debt: two points for none or a clear payoff plan. Irregular costs: two points if sinking funds cover them. Automation: two points if bills and savings run without you.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a scorecard with five rows and small check boxes. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Budget 1
segments.narration: Budget one: a new grad. Forty-eight thousand salary, about thirty-one hundred take-home. Rent fourteen hundred, car and insurance three-fifty, phone and internet one-twenty, student loans two-twenty. Delivery apps: four hundred and ten. Savings: zero. Score: savings zero points. Housing is forty-five percent, one point. No card debt, two points. No sinking funds, zero. Loans on autopay but no savings automation, one point. Four out of ten.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small apartment with takeout bags stacked by the door. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fix 1
segments.narration: The fix. Delivery down to two hundred, and two-ten goes to savings the day after payday. That's about seven percent savings, twenty-five hundred a year. Add a fifty-dollar sinking fund for irregular costs. New score: savings one point, housing one, debt two, irregular two, automation two. Eight out of ten, same paycheck.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. coins moving from a takeout bag into two small jars. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Budget 2
segments.narration: Budget two: a couple. Ninety-five thousand combined. Partner A takes home thirty-eight hundred, Partner B twenty-two hundred. Shared bills twenty-six hundred, split fifty-fifty. B spends fifty-nine percent of their pay on shared bills and runs out every month, sometimes onto a credit card. No joint savings. Score: savings one point, housing two, debt one because a balance is growing, irregular zero, automation one. Five out of ten.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a seesaw tipped heavily to one side with two piggy banks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fix 2
segments.narration: The fix: split by income. A pays about sixty-three percent, B about thirty-seven. Now both keep around fifty-seven percent of their own pay after shared bills. Then both send five percent of take-home to a joint savings account, about three hundred a month, with a named goal. B pays off the card with the breathing room. New score: eight, maybe nine once the card is gone.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the seesaw now level, a shared jar between them filling. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Budget 3
segments.narration: Budget three: a freelancer. Income averages forty-two hundred a month but swings from twenty-five hundred to six thousand. Spending is set for an average month, every month. Low months go on a card. Nothing is set aside for taxes, which means a surprise bill in April. Score: savings zero, housing two, debt zero, irregular zero, automation one. Three out of ten.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a zigzag line with a credit card catching the dips. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fix 3
segments.narration: The fix has three parts. First, all income lands in a holding account. Second, pay yourself a fixed salary of three thousand on the first of each month from it. Third, set aside about a quarter of every payment in a separate tax account and pay quarterly estimated taxes from there. Build the holding account to one or two low months of buffer from the next good month. New score: eight.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a reservoir jar with a steady tap, a separate small tax jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Patterns
segments.narration: Notice the pattern. None of these people had an income problem first. They had a system problem: money with no job gets spent, and costs with no plan go on a card. The fixes were the same three moves every time: automate savings first, give irregular costs a home, and make the hard number visible.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three small gears turning together. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.narration: Score your own budget with the five questions. Seven or more is solid. Under five? Pick the lowest-scoring question and fix only that this month. If you want yours rated in a future episode, send the numbers by DM, no names. We anonymise everything and change details.

script.title: Your first tax return, start to finish
script.hook: 1 afternoon and a few forms. That's what a first tax return really takes. Here's the whole thing, start to finish.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: One afternoon and a few forms. That's what a first tax return really takes. It feels like a big, scary thing, but mostly, it's copying numbers from a few forms into software that does the math. In this video we'll go through the whole process for a simple return: whether you need to file, what to gather, how to file for free, the choices that actually matter, credits people miss, what happens with your refund, and the scams to ignore. This is general education for a simple return, not personal tax advice.
segments.on_screen_text: Your first return, start to finish
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes at a desk with a folder and a laptop, a calm plant nearby. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Do you need to file?
segments.narration: Do you need to file? It depends on your income, filing status and age. If you had taxes withheld from a paycheck, you may want to file even if you're under the limit, because that's how you get withheld money back. Same if you might qualify for the Earned Income Tax Credit, which can pay you even if you owe nothing. The IRS has an interactive tool called 'Do I need to file a tax return?' that answers this in a few minutes.
segments.on_screen_text: Do you need to file? Often worth it anyway
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small signpost with two paths, one leading to a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Gather
segments.narration: Next, gather documents. A W-2 from every job you had last year, even a short summer one. 1099 forms for freelance work, bank interest or payment apps. A 1098-E if you paid student loan interest, a 1098-T if you paid tuition, and a 1095-A if you had marketplace health insurance. Plus your Social Security number, bank details for direct deposit, and last year's return if you filed one.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a folder with several envelopes and a small padlock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Free filing
segments.narration: Now, how to file. For a simple return, you shouldn't need to pay. IRS Free File gives you free brand-name software if your income is under the limit. Start from the IRS website so you land on the free version, not a paid one. VITA offers free in-person help from IRS-certified volunteers if you're under their income limit. And Free File Fillable Forms has no income limit, if you're comfortable with a basic interface.
segments.on_screen_text: File free: Free File, VITA, Fillable Forms
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a laptop with a small government building icon and a green check. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Filing status and dependents
segments.narration: The first important choice is filing status, usually single if you're not married. The second is whether someone can claim you as a dependent. If your parents can claim you, for example as a full-time student under twenty-four they support, you need to check the box saying someone can claim you, and talk to them so both returns agree. Mismatches here are one of the most common reasons first returns get held up.
segments.on_screen_text: Status + dependent box: get these right
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two forms with a connecting arrow and a check mark. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The standard deduction
segments.narration: Next, deductions. Almost everyone in your situation takes the standard deduction, about sixteen thousand one hundred dollars for single filers on 2026 returns. That's income that isn't taxed, and you don't need receipts. You'd only itemize if things like mortgage interest, state taxes and donations added up to more, which is rare for renters. The software compares both for you.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a shield covering the bottom slice of a coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Credits
segments.narration: Then credits, which matter more because they cut your tax dollar for dollar. Look at three. The Earned Income Tax Credit, for workers with lower earnings, including some without kids. The Saver's Credit, if you put money into a 401(k) or IRA and aren't a full-time student or dependent. And education credits, if you paid tuition. Good software asks about each one. Don't skip the questions.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three small gold stars on a form. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Refund or owe
segments.narration: At the end, you'll see a refund or an amount owed. A refund means you had more withheld than you owed. Choose direct deposit, which is the fastest way to get it. If you owe, pay by the April deadline to avoid penalties and interest; IRS Direct Pay is free. If your refund is huge every year, consider adjusting your W-4 so more money comes in each paycheck instead.
segments.on_screen_text: Refund: direct deposit · Owe: pay by April
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a coin returning to a wallet, and a calendar with April circled. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Deadlines
segments.narration: Key dates: W-2s should arrive by the end of January. The filing deadline is usually April fifteenth. If you can't file by then, you can request an extension, but an extension to file isn't an extension to pay. And remember, contributions to an IRA for last year can still be made until that April deadline, which can also help you qualify for the Saver's Credit.
segments.on_screen_text: Dates: late Jan forms · April deadline
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar with two highlighted dates. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Scams
segments.narration: Last thing: scams spike during tax season. The real IRS doesn't text you a refund link, doesn't demand payment in gift cards or crypto, and doesn't threaten immediate arrest. If you're unsure, log in to your IRS online account by typing irs.gov yourself. And consider getting an Identity Protection PIN. It's free and stops anyone else from filing a return using your Social Security number.
segments.on_screen_text: Scams: no texts, no gift cards, get an IP PIN
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a shield in front of a phone with a hook icon. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Check whether you need to file, and file anyway if money was withheld. Gather every W-2 and 1099. File free through IRS Free File, VITA or Fillable Forms. Get your filing status and dependent box right. Take the standard deduction. Don't skip the credit questions. Choose direct deposit, or pay by April if you owe. And ignore anyone who texts you about your refund. That's your first return.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes putting a stamp on an envelope with a small celebratory spark. No text, no logos, no real people.

script.hook: 15.3%. That's the tax most side hustlers don't know about until April. Here's how side income taxes actually work.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Fifteen point three percent. That's the tax most side hustlers don't know about until April, on top of regular income tax. If you drive, deliver, freelance, resell, tutor or sell things you make, this video is the plain-English version of how your side income is taxed: what counts, the forms, self-employment tax, quarterly payments, deductions, and a simple set-aside rule so April isn't a shock. General education, not personal tax advice.

segments.heading: What counts
segments.narration: First, what counts. Money you earn from a business or gig is taxable income, whether or not you get a form. Freelance payments, delivery and rideshare earnings, tips, selling things you make or buy to resell. What generally doesn't count: friends paying you back for dinner, and selling your own used stuff for less than you paid. Label personal transfers as personal in payment apps to keep things clean.
segments.on_screen_text: Gig income: taxable, form or not
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a coin stack with or without a form, both under a small tax gate. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The forms
segments.narration: The forms. A 1099-NEC comes from a client who paid you six hundred dollars or more. A 1099-K comes from payment apps and online marketplaces; after changes in 2025, the federal reporting threshold is generally over twenty thousand dollars and two hundred transactions, though some states are lower. Either way, the form is just a report. You owe tax on all the income, including income no form shows.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two small envelopes from an office building and a phone. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Self-employment tax
segments.narration: Now the surprise. At a regular job, your employer pays half of Social Security and Medicare and withholds the other half. When you work for yourself, you pay both halves: self-employment tax, fifteen point three percent of your net earnings, roughly. Example: if you net ten thousand from deliveries after expenses, self-employment tax is around fourteen hundred, before any income tax. You do get to deduct half of it when figuring income tax, which softens it a little.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a coin tower with two thin slices peeled off. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Quarterly payments
segments.narration: Because nobody withholds tax from gig income, the IRS generally expects you to pay during the year if you'll owe a thousand dollars or more. These are quarterly estimated payments, due in April, June, September and January. You pay through IRS Direct Pay or your IRS online account and mark them as estimated tax. If you also have a regular job, another option is raising the withholding on your W-4 to cover the side income.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a calendar with four small envelopes spaced out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Safe harbor
segments.narration: How much to pay each quarter? A common safe harbor: if you pay at least as much as your total tax from last year, spread over the four quarters, you generally avoid the underpayment penalty, even if you end up owing more in April. If your income was over a hundred fifty thousand, it's a hundred and ten percent. The IRS Form 1040-ES worksheet walks you through it.
segments.on_screen_text: Safe harbor: pay last year's tax in 4 parts
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small umbrella over four coin stacks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Deductions
segments.narration: Now the good part: deductions. You're taxed on profit, not revenue. Common business expenses include supplies, a phone or internet share used for the work, software, platform fees, and for drivers, either actual car expenses or the standard mileage rate. Mileage adds up fast, so track every work trip. Expenses must be ordinary and necessary for the work, and personal use doesn't count.
segments.on_screen_text: Taxed on profit: track expenses + mileage
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a receipt, a small car with a route line, and a toolbox. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Records
segments.narration: Records make all of this easy. Keep a simple spreadsheet with four columns: date, who paid you or what you bought, amount, and a note. Use a separate checking account for the side hustle so business money doesn't blend with personal. Snap photos of receipts. For mileage, a log with date, start, end and purpose, or a mileage app. Ten minutes a week beats a weekend of panic in April.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a simple spreadsheet grid and a second small bank card. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Set-aside rule
segments.narration: The rule that keeps April calm: every time side income lands, move twenty-five to thirty percent into a separate tax savings account the same day. That covers self-employment tax and a typical income tax bracket for many people. Pay your quarterly estimates from that account. If there's money left after you file, that's a bonus, not a bill.
segments.on_screen_text: Set aside 25–30% the day it lands

segments.heading: When to get help
segments.narration: When should you get help? If your side income is growing fast, you have employees, you sell physical inventory, or you're unsure about a deduction, a one-time session with a tax professional can pay for itself. Look for an enrolled agent or CPA, and check credentials. VITA volunteers can't handle every self-employment situation, so ask first.
segments.on_screen_text: Growing fast? Talk to a pro once

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. All gig income is taxable, form or not. 1099-NEC is from clients, 1099-K from apps and marketplaces. Self-employment tax is about fifteen point three percent of net earnings. Pay quarterly if you'll owe a thousand or more, using last year's tax as a safe harbor. Track expenses and mileage, because you're taxed on profit. Use a separate account. And set aside twenty-five to thirty percent of every payment the day it lands.
